prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
Apollo 13 left the Kennedy Space Center on 11 April 1970 with three men aboard: James Lovell, the commander, John Swigert, the command module pilot, and Fred Haise, the lunar module pilot. Swigert was a late replacement. Ken Mattingly had been due to fly, but he was exposed to German measles and doctors found he had no immunity, so he was taken off the crew two days before launch. The mission was meant to be the third landing on the Moon, in the Fra Mauro highlands. The launch went mostly to plan, though the centre engine of the second stage shut down early and the remaining engines burned longer to make up the speed. The command and service module was named Odyssey and the lunar module was named Aquarius.

The first two days were uneventful. On the evening of 13 April, about 56 hours into the flight and roughly 320,000 kilometres from Earth, Houston asked the crew to stir the supercold oxygen and hydrogen stored in tanks in the service module. This was a routine task that keeps the contents from settling and keeps the quantity gauges accurate. A little after nine o'clock Houston time, Swigert switched on the fans in oxygen tank 2. Within a minute there was a bang and the spacecraft shuddered. Swigert reported, "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here," and Lovell repeated it a moment later. The instruments showed a drop in electrical voltage, and then a steady fall in the pressure of the oxygen tanks.

The investigation that followed traced the fault to the tank itself. It had been knocked slightly when it was lifted out of an earlier spacecraft in 1968. Before launch, ground crews ran its heaters for a long time at a higher voltage than the thermostat switches were built for, and this damaged the insulation on the wires inside. When the fans started, a spark ignited that insulation, the pressure rose, and the tank failed. The blast tore off a panel of the service module and damaged the second oxygen tank. Within about three hours both tanks had lost their oxygen. The oxygen fed the fuel cells that supplied the command module with electricity and water, so Odyssey was left with only its batteries, which were meant for the last hours of the flight.

Within an hour, controllers and crew accepted that the command module could not be kept running. Lovell and Haise moved into Aquarius, which had its own oxygen, water and power. It had been built to support two men for about two days on the lunar surface, and it now had to support three men for four days. The landing was abandoned. The spacecraft was not on a path that would bring it home on its own, because earlier in the flight it had been steered away from the safest route to reach Fra Mauro. About five hours after the explosion the crew used the lunar module's descent engine to put it back on a path that would swing round the Moon and return toward Earth. After passing behind the Moon, they burned the same engine again for about four and a half minutes. This shortened the trip by roughly ten hours and moved the planned landing to the Pacific Ocean, where recovery ships were stationed. At its farthest point the spacecraft was about 400,000 kilometres from Earth, a distance no one has travelled to before or since.

Living in Aquarius was hard. To save power, the crew switched off nearly everything, including most of the heating. The cabin temperature fell to about 3 degrees Celsius and water condensed on the walls. Each man received around 180 millilitres of water a day, and the crew ate little. Haise developed a fever from a urinary infection, which doctors thought was linked to the shortage of water. Together the three men lost nearly 14 kilograms. They slept very little, because it was too cold and too noisy with the equipment that remained on.

A more immediate problem was carbon dioxide. The lunar module removed the gas from the cabin air with canisters of lithium hydroxide, but it carried only enough for two men for two days. The command module had spare canisters, but they were square and the lunar module's system took round ones. Engineers on the ground built an adapter from the materials the crew had on board, which were a plastic bag, a piece of cardboard from a flight manual cover, a hose from a spacesuit and duct tape. They read the instructions to the crew over the radio, and the crew assembled it on 14 April. Carbon dioxide levels in the cabin then began to fall. Many people have described this improvised part as the best-known example of the work done on the ground, and that is a view, but the record shows that it was one of many problems solved in a few days.

Another group worked on how to bring the command module back to life. Odyssey's batteries had to last through re-entry, so the crew could not use them at all until the last hours. Mattingly and others tested a new start-up procedure in a simulator, with a fixed limit on the electrical current it could draw. The final version differed a good deal from the normal checklist. It was read to Swigert and Lovell when the time came.

The path home also needed small corrections. Without a working guidance system aligned in the normal way, the crew had to point the spacecraft by hand. For the last correction on 17 April, Lovell lined up Aquarius using the line between night and day on the Earth, and the engine burned for 14 seconds. About four and a half hours before re-entry the crew separated the service module. Lovell looked out of the window and reported that one whole side of the spacecraft was missing. The photographs they took showed the panel gone and the damage around it, which gave the engineers on the ground their first clear sight of what had happened. Swigert, Haise and Lovell then moved back into Odyssey, started it using the new procedure, and released Aquarius about an hour before they entered the atmosphere.

Re-entry was the last risk. Controllers did not know whether the explosion had damaged the heat shield on the command module. During re-entry, the heat of the air around the capsule blocks radio signals. This blackout was expected to last about three minutes, and it lasted about a minute longer than that. Many people waited at the mission control and elsewhere without any word from the crew. Then Joe Kerwin, speaking from Houston, heard the crew answer. The parachutes opened and the capsule landed in the South Pacific, near Samoa, at about midday Houston time on 17 April, a few kilometres from the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima. The flight had lasted nearly 143 hours.

A review board chaired by Edgar Cortright reported on the cause. Its recommendations led to a redesign of the oxygen tanks, changes to the heaters and thermostats, and an extra oxygen tank and an additional battery in the service module. The programme paused for several months. Apollo 14 flew in January 1971 and landed at Fra Mauro, the site Apollo 13 had been meant to reach. The mission control team received the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Lovell, Swigert and Haise had not landed on the Moon, but all three came home alive.
